It reaches 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg val without additional segmentation-specific training. Backend model updates can improve accuracy without retraining the pipeline. The code is available at https://abdullahamdi.com/llmseg .
bullets: Addresses whether MLLMs can directly produce image masks without segmentation-specific architecture, annotations, or training.
Uses three stages: detect queried instances, trace confined closed B-splines with optional holes, and refine residual errors iteratively.
Produces binary masks with inspectable intermediate geometric representations.
Evaluated on referring, reasoning, open-vocabulary instance, semantic segmentation, and zero-shot detection benchmarks.
With Gemini-3.7-Flash, it reports 71.5 cIoU on ReasonSeg validation and is competitive with or often surpasses SAM 3 on identical items.
papers.selection_reason: Develops LLMSeg, a training-free pipeline that enables vision-capable LLMs to perform image segmentation using B-splines, demonstrating strong open-vocabulary performance without task-specific training.
papers.title: LLMSeg: Training-Free Text-Prompted Image Segmentation with B-Splines
papers.tldr: LLMSeg turns a general-purpose vision-language model into a training-free text-prompted image segmenter using iterative B-spline geometry instead of a segmentation head or decoder.

papers.abstract: Interactive video world models predict how an environment evolves under user actions, but most existing systems assume one controlled agent and one task-specific action interface. We study multi-agent video world modeling, where one model generates a joint visual future for multiple controlled agents while interpreting heterogeneous controls ranging from binary game buttons to continuous robot commands. This task presents two complementary challenges. First, every agent-indexed action stream must control its intended visual entity independently. Second, the model must adapt the meaning of each control variable across different tasks, where the same tensor dimension may denote an attack, steering command, or robot command. We introduce LiveAct, centered on a Heterogeneous Action Interface (HAI) whose two components mirror this decomposition. To support independent control, Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation uses language-driven spatial gates and agent-specific attention to bind each action stream to its intended visual agent. To accommodate heterogeneous controls, Schema-Guided Action Adaptation describes each control variable in language and modulates its semantic token with the synchronized numerical value. We further transfer the complete interface to a blockwise causal generator through teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching, enabling efficient streaming generation while retaining agent-specific control and action semantics. We instantiate the formulation on six multi-agent sources spanning games and multi-robot manipulation, and evaluate visual quality, action following, agent attribution, and latency. Across games and robot manipulation, LiveAct reaches 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy without agent locations or identity crops, and the causal generator attains 17.70 FPS at $512\times 448$.
authors: Xinyu Wang, Huafeng Shi, Yue Ma, Zijie Meng, Teng Xi, Yuzhuo Chen, Yucheng Wang, Ruicheng Zhang, Guoxin Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Xiu Li, Fangneng Zhan
bullets: Addresses multi-agent world models that must bind each action stream to the correct visual agent and interpret task-dependent controls.
Introduces a Heterogeneous Action Interface combining Agent-Aware Spatial Modulation with Schema-Guided Action Adaptation.
Transfers the interface to a blockwise causal generator using teacher forcing and rollout-aware distribution matching for streaming generation.
Evaluated across six game and multi-robot manipulation sources on visual quality, action following, attribution, and latency.
Achieves 0.898 and 0.942 agent-attribution accuracy and 17.70 FPS generation at 512×448, without agent locations or identity crops.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces LiveAct, a multi-agent interactive video world model with a Heterogeneous Action Interface, directly fitting the World Models taxonomy.
papers.title: LiveAct: Towards Real-Time Multi-Agent World Models with Heterogeneous Action Interfaces
papers.tldr: LiveAct enables real-time multi-agent video world modeling with independent control of multiple agents and heterogeneous action interfaces across games and robot tasks.

papers.abstract: 3D semantic occupancy prediction estimates voxel-wise occupancy and semantic labels throughout a scene. Our experiments reveal that conventional sparse transposed-convolution upsampling yields poorly differentiated voxel responses and that successive decoder layers discard previously correct semantic predictions. To address these issues, we present Feature-Diverse Upsampling and Memory-Aware Decoding for 3D Occupancy Prediction (FM-Occ), comprising two components. First, 3D Sparse Subvoxel Shuffle (3S) mitigates feature homogenization by constructing candidate child features in the channel dimension, jointly transforming and normalizing them, and then rearranging them onto a finer sparse grid with explicit feature-coordinate correspondence. Second, Entropy-Regulated Layer-wise Memory (ER-LM) retains semantic information across decoder layers by maintaining a layer-wise memory for each query through gated recurrent updates and using prediction entropy to regulate the historical information propagated to the next layer. During training, a class-weighted entropy loss Lcwe provides label-guided regularization for matched semantic queries. On SemanticKITTI, 3S increases the spatial coefficient of variation of normalized voxel-wise root-mean-square (RMS) responses from 0.41% to 4.03%, while ER-LM reduces semantic degradation and improves error correction across decoder layers. The combined FM-Occ improves mIoU from 12.16% to 12.73% with negligible memory overhead. ER-LM further improves mIoU in the BEV-based DISC framework from 16.78% to 17.17%, supporting its applicability across 3D voxel-based and BEV-based architectures.
authors: Yujia Zhai (Great Bay University), Guoming Huang (Great Bay University), Zhuanghuai Wang (Great Bay University), Bangquan Xie (Great Bay University)
bullets: Addresses feature homogenization from sparse transposed-convolution upsampling and semantic degradation during decoding.
Introduces 3D Sparse Subvoxel Shuffle (3S), which generates and rearranges candidate child features onto a finer sparse grid.
Introduces Entropy-Regulated Layer-wise Memory (ER-LM), using gated memory and prediction entropy to retain and regulate historical semantic information.
On SemanticKITTI, FM-Occ raises mIoU from 12.16% to 12.73% with negligible memory overhead; ER-LM also improves DISC from 16.78% to 17.17%.
Scope: evaluated across voxel-based and BEV-based 3D occupancy architectures.
papers.selection_reason: 3D occupancy prediction with memory-aware decoding, relevant to 3D perception and robot navigation architectures.
papers.title: FM-Occ: Feature-Diverse Upsampling and Memory-Aware Decoding for 3D Occupancy Prediction
papers.tldr: FM-Occ improves 3D semantic occupancy prediction by diversifying sparse upsampling features and preserving semantic information across decoder layers.

papers.abstract: Language models relying on verbalized Chain-of-Thought (CoT) are constrained to token-by-token generation in the language space, where many tokens serve textual coherence rather than core reasoning. This entangles genuine differences in logical trajectories with superficial variations in verbalization. Moving reasoning into a compact, continuous latent space offers a promising alternative for efficiently representing and exploring diverse reasoning trajectories. However, current latent models remain largely deterministic, capturing only a single reasoning trajectory rather than modeling a distribution over multiple valid alternatives. While stochastic approaches parameterize distributions over latent reasoning steps, they frequently suffer from unstable optimization and limited empirical performance. Furthermore, their reliance on autoregressive latent prediction during training precludes effective parallelization, leading to prohibitively long training times. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for probabilistic latent reasoning. PLRM adopts a JEPA-style objective in which the posterior infers latent distributions in parallel from observed reasoning trajectories, while the prior learns to predict the subsequent latent distribution via teacher forcing. To model heterogeneous reasoning processes, we introduce a discrete strategy variable together with a mixture-based prior, allowing the model to preserve the Gaussian-mixture structure induced by multiple distinct reasoning trajectories rather than collapsing them into a single Gaussian. Across diverse benchmarks, PLRM achieves performance competitive with deterministic latent reasoning models on single-trajectory datasets while enabling efficient training and consistently outperforming competing stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory datasets.
authors: Seokhyun Lee, Seongjun Lee, Changhee Lee
bullets: Addresses the limitations of token-level CoT and deterministic latent reasoning, which obscure or fail to represent diverse logical trajectories.
Uses a JEPA-style objective with parallel posterior inference and teacher-forced prior prediction to avoid autoregressive latent training.
Introduces a discrete strategy variable and mixture-based prior to preserve heterogeneous reasoning modes instead of collapsing them into one Gaussian.
Matches deterministic latent-reasoning performance on single-trajectory benchmarks and consistently outperforms stochastic baselines on multi-trajectory benchmarks.
The approach is evaluated across diverse benchmarks, with scope focused on latent reasoning and trajectory diversity.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes Probabilistic Latent Reasoning Models (PLRM), a parallelizable variational framework for modeling diverse reasoning trajectories in latent space to improve efficiency and diversity.
papers.title: Parallelizable Probabilistic Latent Reasoning for Diverse Reasoning Trajectories
papers.tldr: PLRM is a parallelizable variational latent-reasoning framework that models multiple valid reasoning trajectories more efficiently and effectively than prior stochastic approaches.

papers.abstract: We propose a novel stochastic cascading bandit setup where probing an ordered shortlist of $K$ out of $L$ arms incurs position-dependent costs, and the learner observes only noisy feedback regarding each arm's true output. We identify a sub-class of noise models for which the optimal shortlist can be found by sorting arms according to a per-arm score: such a score exists for both selection and ordering when the channel has no false positives, and for ordering alone (but not selection) when measurements are costless; however in general neither selection nor ordering is separable once noise and cost are both present. For the case where both selection and ordering scores exist, we provide a UCB-based algorithm with $O((L-K)\log T)$ instance-dependent regret over a time horizon $T$, which matches an algorithm-agnostic lower bound (up to constant factors). For the more challenging scenario where scores don't exist, we develop a new algorithmic template, DP-UCB, that embeds optimism directly inside an exact dynamic program, yielding $O\big(LK\log T\big)$ regret. Finally, we validate our theoretical results through extensive numerical evaluations and simulations over both synthetic and real-world datasets.
bullets: Studies when the optimal shortlist and ordering can be determined by per-arm scores under different noise and cost conditions.
Introduces a UCB algorithm with instance-dependent O((L−K) log T) regret when both selection and ordering are score-separable.
Proposes DP-UCB, which integrates optimism into an exact dynamic program for non-separable settings, achieving O(LK log T) regret.
Provides a matching algorithm-agnostic lower bound up to constants in the score-separable case.
Validates the theoretical results through simulations and experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes online cascading bandit algorithms with regret guarantees, fitting continual/online learning.
papers.title: Cascading Bandits with Noisy Observations: Algorithms and Regret Bounds
papers.tldr: This paper develops algorithms and regret guarantees for cascading bandits with position-dependent probing costs and noisy feedback, including a dynamic-programming approach when simple arm rankings fail.

papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) aims to recover reasoning capabilities in low-bit large language models (LLMs). Existing recipes typically supervise the quantized student with the original full-precision model on fixed response sequences. However, the resulting low-bit quantized models still struggle on long-horizon reasoning tasks and often fail to terminate within a token budget that suffices for the full-precision model. We identify two challenges in closing this gap. First, fixed-response supervision leaves a mismatch between training prefixes and those encountered during student generation, and this trajectory divergence grows as responses lengthen. Second, on its own prefixes, the student underpredicts some next-token candidates and overpredicts others, and this distributional misalignment becomes more frequent at high-entropy prefixes. We present OnQ, a low-bit recovery pipeline that combines on-policy distillation and candidate-wise Dynamic KL. Starting from block-wise calibration, the quantized student generates responses and receives full-precision teacher supervision on its own prefixes. Dynamic KL weights forward and reverse KL by each candidate's teacher-student probability ratio to balance correction of under- and overprediction. Across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, OnQ achieves the highest nine-benchmark average, with the largest gains on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks. At 2 bits, it outperforms every baseline on every benchmark at every model size, improving the Qwen3-8B average by 10.26 points over the strongest baseline. It also produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitive errors.
authors: Boyuan Zheng, Jing Xiong, Chenwei Wu, Hui Shen, Zesen Zhao, Hei Ting Una Chan, Xueshen Liu, Zhen Zhang, Liyue Shen, Zechun Liu, Z. Morley Mao
bullets: Fixed-response QAT creates a training–generation trajectory mismatch that worsens for longer reasoning sequences.
The quantized student also miscalibrates next-token probabilities, especially at high-entropy prefixes.
OnQ combines block-wise calibration, on-policy distillation, and candidate-wise Dynamic KL to correct under- and overprediction.
Across Qwen3 1.7B–8B at 2- and 3-bit precision, it achieves the best nine-benchmark average, with particularly large long-horizon reasoning gains.
At 2 bits, it beats all baselines on every benchmark and produces shorter responses with fewer truncations and repetitions.
papers.selection_reason: Recovers reasoning in low-bit quantized LLMs via on-policy distillation and dynamic KL, improving efficiency of deployed language models.
papers.title: Right On Q: Recovering Reasoning under Quantization via Self-Generated Trajectories
papers.tldr: OnQ recovers long-horizon reasoning in low-bit LLMs by distilling teacher behavior on the quantized student’s own trajectories with adaptive KL correction.

papers.abstract: Learning-based path planners based on diffusion and flow matching can generate diverse trajectories from demonstrations but typically lack mechanisms for constraint satisfaction and collision avoidance during deployment. This work proposes a framework that combines flow-matching-based path planning with model predictive path-following control to integrate data-driven path generation with real-time, constraint-aware execution. The flow-matching model captures multimodal path distributions, while the predictive controller adapts motion online to satisfy state and input constraints and avoid obstacles using updated local sensor information. An event-triggered re-planning scheme incorporates predictive control solutions into subsequent path generation, promoting collision-free navigation in environments with previously unseen obstacles. Simulation results for mobile robot navigation demonstrate robust performance across cluttered environments. The framework provides a systematic approach to combining flow matching with predictive control for adaptive, data-driven navigation.
authors: Philipp Holzmann, Maik Pfefferkorn, Joao Carvalho, Ali Younes, An Thai Le, Georgia Chalvatzaki, Jan Peters, Rolf Findeisen
bullets: Addresses the lack of constraint satisfaction and collision avoidance in learning-based trajectory planners.
Uses flow matching to generate diverse, multimodal paths from demonstrations.
Applies model predictive path-following control for real-time adaptation to state/input constraints and local obstacles.
Employs event-triggered replanning to incorporate control updates and respond to previously unseen obstacles.
Simulations show robust mobile-robot navigation in cluttered environments.
papers.selection_reason: Combines flow-matching path generation with predictive control for learned, constraint-aware robot navigation.
papers.title: Integrating Flow Matching and Model Predictive Control for Safe Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: A flow-matching planner paired with predictive control enables adaptive robot navigation that accounts for constraints and newly detected obstacles.

papers.abstract: Robots deployed in human-centered environments need maps that support both geometric navigation and open-vocabulary semantic queries beyond a fixed label set. A key challenge is enriching such maps with semantic information without relying on manually annotated segmentation masks or closed-set semantic categories. Existing geometry-driven active mapping maximizes coverage but treats semantics as a passive by-product of the collected trajectory, whereas active semantic mapping typically depends on supervised semantic segmentation. We present AOV-GS, an active 3D Gaussian mapping system that guides exploration using frozen foundation models. During coarse exploration, AOV-GS re-ranks geometrically promising candidate views according to CLIP mask-embedding novelty computed from SAM instance segmentation, biasing exploration toward semantically informative regions. Frozen SAM and CLIP provide instance masks and language-aligned embeddings throughout mapping, while a lightweight scene-specific language field is fitted offline directly to the collected CLIP embeddings rather than manually annotated masks, enabling open-vocabulary text-query segmentation on novel views. In a controlled comparison using the same SAM-CLIP perception stack, AOV-GS improves average language-field mIoU over geometry-only active planning by 1.3 percentage points on Replica (34.6% on eight scenes) and by 1.8 points on Matterport3D (23.1% on five scenes). With CorrCLIP, AOV-GS reaches 35.6% on Replica, 2.0 points above the matched Geometry-based + CorrCLIP baseline. Novel-view PSNR remains comparable to the geometry-only baseline on both datasets while depth L1 improves on Replica. Code is available at https://github.com/OptimusFaber/AOV-GS.
authors: Rodion Shkokov, Tatiana Zemskova, Dmitry Yudin
bullets: Targets robot maps that support both geometric navigation and language-based semantic queries beyond fixed label sets.
Re-ranks candidate views using CLIP embedding novelty from SAM instance masks, complementing geometry-driven exploration.
Fits a lightweight scene-specific language field directly to frozen SAM-CLIP embeddings for text-query segmentation on novel views.
Improves language-field mIoU over matched geometry-only planning by 1.3 points on Replica and 1.8 points on Matterport3D.
Maintains comparable novel-view PSNR and improves depth L1 on Replica; evaluation covers eight Replica and five Matterport3D scenes.
papers.selection_reason: Active open-vocabulary semantic mapping using 3D Gaussian Splatting, directly relevant to embodied AI navigation and 3D foundation models.
papers.title: AOV-GS: Active Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping with 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.tldr: AOV-GS actively explores environments for semantically informative views, enabling open-vocabulary 3D Gaussian maps without manual segmentation annotations.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents powered by foundation models can reason, plan, and use tools, but their fixed weights and context limits hinder sustained learning from experience over long-term deployment. While external memory systems attempt to bridge this gap, they mostly act as passive retrieval caches, evaluated primarily by whether they can recall stored facts or past interactions. Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question. In this paper, we introduce Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), arguing that memory should be judged by whether it improves future actions, not merely what it retrieves. MCCL has three main parts. First, a three-axis taxonomy organizes memory by where state is stored (substrates), what form it takes (assets), and how it is managed (policies). This defines a two-loop lifecycle that updates memory state in an inner loop while refining management policies in an outer loop based on task feedback. Second, an evaluation protocol measures retention under interference, adaptation to change, and task transfer to isolate genuine behavioral gains from simple context expansion. Third, a memory scaling framework models how agent performance scales with experience, storage capacity, and compute budgets across non-parametric and parametric memory. Together, these components reframe agent memory from passive lookup to continuous learning, offering a principled route toward self-improving autonomous agents.
authors: Dongfang Li, Zhuoen Chen, Bonian Jia, Zixuan Liu, Zhengxuan Lu, Can Deng, Yukun Shi, Yuhang Meng, Xin Zhang, Jiahe Huang, Fuhao Li, Junmai Wang, Shunyao Wen, Jingjun Sun, Jiaxu Tian, Jiangling Zhang, Zihan Wang, Liangyou Li, Yitong Yao, Shuangyong Song, Beilun Wang, Pengxu Wei, Hanlin Xu, Chang Liu, Yongxiang Li, Baotian Hu, Xiangyang Ji, Min Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Fixed model weights and limited context hinder agents’ long-term learning from experience.
Method: A taxonomy categorizes memory by storage substrate, asset type, and management policy within a two-loop update lifecycle.
Evaluation: The protocol tests retention under interference, adaptation to change, and transfer across tasks.
Framework: A scaling model relates performance to experience, memory capacity, and compute across non-parametric and parametric memory.
Contribution: The paper provides a principled framework for evaluating and designing memory-driven self-improving agents.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Memory-Centric Continual Learning (MCCL), a framework that redefines memory evaluation based on behavioral improvement and future action quality rather than simple retrieval.
papers.title: Memory-Centric Continual Learning for AI Agents
papers.tldr: MCCL reframes agent memory as a mechanism for continual behavioral improvement rather than passive retrieval.

papers.abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) models improve scalability by routing input tokens to only a subset of expert networks, but they often suffer from representation collapse, in which multiple experts converge toward similar functions and lose their intended diversity. Prior work has addressed this limitation either by improving router architectures or by introducing auxiliary loss terms that implicitly penalize similarity among experts. However, router-based approaches remain vulnerable to routing collapses, and loss-based approaches can conflict with the task's original objective during optimization. In this work, we propose GaP-MoE (Gradient Accumulation and Projection in MoE), which induces expert specialization by directly manipulating expert output gradients rather than modifying the loss function. At each training step, GaP-MoE stochastically selects one of the $TopK$ routed experts as a leader based on normalized routing scores, and projects the gradients of the remaining follower experts onto the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by the leader's recent gradients. This removes directional overlap between expert gradients without altering the task loss, allowing specialization to emerge as a direct consequence of the optimization dynamics rather than an externally imposed constraint. We evaluate GaP-MoE in both fine-tuning settings (BERT-based, on GLUE) and from-scratch pretraining settings (GPT-2-based, on WikiText-103, enwik8, and text8), and further confirm its compatibility as a drop-in module for existing SMoE architectures. Experimental results show that GaP-MoE achieves performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.
bullets: Addresses expert representation collapse, where multiple MoE experts learn similar functions.
Selects a routed leader expert using normalized routing scores and accumulates its recent gradients.
Projects follower-expert gradients onto the orthogonal complement of the leader-gradient subspace.
Encourages specialization without changing the task loss or relying on router modifications.
Evaluated in BERT fine-tuning and GPT-2 pretraining settings, achieving performance comparable to or better than standard SMoE.
papers.selection_reason: Improves expert specialization in sparse mixture-of-experts LLMs, directly relevant to modern LLM architectures.
papers.title: GaP-MoE : Explicit Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts via Orthogonal Gradient Accumulation and Projection
papers.tldr: GaP-MoE promotes diverse expert behavior in sparse MoE models by orthogonally projecting follower-expert gradients away from a selected leader’s recent gradient directions.

papers.abstract: Mid-training (MT) is a training phase in LLM training pipelines that continues pretraining (PT) on smaller datasets of higher value. Taking the PT and MT phases as a whole, training usually starts with only PT data and then transitions completely to MT data. In this work, we view this complete transition from PT to MT data as a special case of a broader class of data mixing schedules that specify how the proportions of PT and MT tokens in each batch change over training. Under fixed total training compute and MT token budgets, we ask: Is this complete transition to MT data optimal for minimizing final MT loss? We show that the answer depends on the learning rate (LR) schedule: one data schedule may outperform another under one LR schedule, but changing only the LR schedule can reverse the outcome. Specifically, when the LR decays throughout continued training, introducing MT data earlier and mixing it with PT data lowers the final MT loss compared with placing all MT data at the end of training, but this result is reversed if we use constant LR. We therefore study how to jointly choose when to introduce MT data and when to decay the LR through ablation studies, and find that it is better to decay the LR only after MT data enters training. Finally, we develop a theoretical model that explains why the optimal data schedule for a fixed MT token budget depends on the LR schedule.
authors: Haodong Wen, Kairong Luo, Tingkai Yan, Wenguang Chen, Kaifeng Lyu
bullets: The study asks whether switching completely from pretraining (PT) data to mid-training (MT) data is optimal under fixed compute and MT-token budgets.
With a decaying learning rate, introducing and mixing MT data earlier improves final MT loss versus placing all MT data at the end.
With a constant learning rate, this comparison reverses, showing that schedule choices are interdependent.
Ablations suggest delaying learning-rate decay until after MT data enters training is preferable.
A theoretical model explains why the optimal data schedule depends on the learning-rate schedule.
papers.selection_reason: Studies joint data and learning-rate schedules for LLM mid-training, relevant to LLM training and foundation-model development.
papers.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together
papers.tldr: Data-mixing and learning-rate schedules interact strongly in mid-training, so they should be designed jointly rather than independently.

papers.abstract: A transformer MLP gives each hidden channel two roles: a reader that decides when the channel responds, and a writer that decides what it adds back to the residual stream. Read as a key--value memory, the layer can be measured one factor set at a time: the pairing of readers to writers is carried only by their shared index, invisible to any quantity computed from one factor set alone. Yet training couples the two factors through their joint update, so we ask what reading them together shows. The block supplies the joint instrument: the MLP writes back into the very stream it reads, so the exact Jacobian of its update is square, and its agreement with its own transpose resolves into reader--writer terms whose inner products give each channel, read as a couple, a signed pairing coordinate. Ranked by this coordinate, each block we measure has a small core of strongly coupled channels; where initialization gives either sign equally, the core is nearly all opposed: each writer points against the direction its reader responds to. This opposed core recurs from the smallest models trained from scratch to released checkpoints; its sign is in place within a few percent of training and holds while the coupling grows. Read as couples, most channels return their contribution against the reader that fired it, and the readers of later blocks take it up; few show in the logits. Training holds the couples in place: flipping the opposed writers moves the output toward common tokens, and a writer permuted onto another reader regrows to fit that reader while the reader stays.
authors: Giyeong Oh, Sunghee Ahn, Youngjae Yu
bullets: Treating readers and writers jointly reveals coupling that is invisible when either factor set is analyzed alone.
The MLP’s exact square Jacobian is compared with its transpose to derive a signed reader–writer pairing coordinate for each channel.
Across models and checkpoints, strongly coupled cores are usually opposed: writers point against the directions that activate their readers.
Most channels return contributions against the reader that triggered them, while later blocks can take up these contributions; few appear directly in the logits.
Perturbations support functional coupling: flipping opposed writers shifts outputs toward common tokens, and permuting a writer onto another reader causes it to regrow to fit that reader.
papers.selection_reason: Analyzes transformer MLP reader-writer coupling, relevant to LLM architecture and interpretability.
papers.title: Reader--Writer Coupling in Transformer MLPs
papers.tldr: Transformer MLP channels form coupled reader–writer pairs, with a small, rapidly established core whose writers typically oppose the directions their readers detect.

papers.abstract: Knowledge graph question generation (KGQG) generates natural-language questions from structured graph evidence and a target answer. When the input graph is temporal, a valid question must also preserve the answer field, time condition, reference event, and temporal order that determine the answer set. Existing KGQG methods and prompting baselines can produce fluent questions that alter these conditions, causing temporal semantic drift. This paper studies temporal KGQG as a constraint-preserving graph-to-question problem and proposes ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented and constraint-aware generation framework. ChronoSynth first constructs a Temporal Intent State to make the intended question semantics explicit. It then retrieves compatible typed question patterns from an indexed pattern memory, adapts them to the input graph, and validates the generated question. Validation feedback guides revisions when a supported inconsistency is detected. Experiments on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ demonstrate state-of-the-art generation performance, with ablations supporting the contributions of its components.
authors: Feng Liang, Weixin Zeng, Runhao Zhao, Mingjun Zhou, Shaoshi Yang, Xiang Zhao
bullets: Targets temporal semantic drift in KG question generation, where questions may alter the answer field, time condition, reference event, or temporal order.
Builds a Temporal Intent State to explicitly represent the intended question semantics.
Retrieves compatible typed question patterns, adapts them to the graph, and validates the generated question.
Uses validation feedback to revise questions when supported inconsistencies are detected.
Achieves state-of-the-art generation performance on CRONQUESTIONS and MultiTQ; ablations support its component contributions.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces ChronoSynth, a memory-augmented framework for temporal knowledge graph question generation that preserves temporal constraints during generation.
papers.title: ChronoSynth: Constraint-Aware Question Synthesis over Temporal Knowledge Graphs
papers.tldr: ChronoSynth generates fluent questions from temporal knowledge graphs while preserving the constraints that determine their answers.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied across the scientific discovery pipeline, from synthesizing literature to generating hypotheses to informing experimental design. A unifying principle behind these tasks is the need to continuously update beliefs as evidence accumulates, for which Bayesian inference provides a natural framework. However, existing work assumes that LLMs cannot carry out principled Bayesian belief updating in context, instead relying on simplifications and heuristics. To challenge this assumption, we present a principled evaluation of Bayesian reasoning capabilities in LLMs, analyzing both the model's internal consistency as well as its ability to recover an externally determined posterior. Specifically, we build an evaluation framework spanning qualitative epistemological examples to probe probabilistic coherence, quantitative benchmarks of Bayesian inference capabilities, and analyses of the impact of non-Bayesian updates on downstream task performance. Across different scenarios, we find that LLMs generally violate Bayes' rule when updating their beliefs in context. However, when equipped with modern reasoning abilities and code execution capabilities, their performance drastically improves, enabling even the close approximation of analytically intractable posteriors. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs with access to appropriate tools could already be used to make complex belief updates in scientific discovery, enabling rapid acceleration of the efficiency and scale of AI-powered scientific discovery.
authors: Linus Filbry, Luckeciano C. Melo, Yarin Gal
bullets: Evaluates whether LLMs can perform principled Bayesian belief updating in context.
Tests probabilistic coherence, quantitative inference, and effects of non-Bayesian updates on downstream tasks.
Finds that LLMs generally violate Bayes’ rule during belief updates.
Reasoning abilities and code execution markedly improve performance, including on analytically intractable posteriors.
Suggests tool-equipped LLMs may support complex belief updates in scientific discovery.
papers.selection_reason: LLM Bayesian belief updating and posterior recovery evaluation; aligns with language foundation model reasoning interests.
papers.title: From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context?
papers.tldr: LLM agents often update beliefs non-Bayesianly, but reasoning and code tools can substantially improve their ability to approximate complex posteriors.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires a robot to remember task-relevant information beyond its short observation window. Existing memory-augmented policies typically retrieve relevant information from history and reason over it at execution time, placing a heavy reasoning burden on the high-level model. To address this challenge, we propose PAL (\textbf{P}lan first, \textbf{A}ct \textbf{L}ater), a hierarchical memory framework for vision-language robot manipulation. It maintains a short-term visual buffer, a semantic-event memory, and an executable \texttt{subtask\_list}. A high-level vision-language model (VLM) converts streaming visual observations into the \texttt{subtask\_list}. At execution time, the VLM selects the currently relevant subtask from the \texttt{subtask\_list} and passes it to a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy. To teach the model what to write to memory and when to update it, we introduce a two-stage data generation procedure that first expands sparse update supervision and then uses self-labeling with task-grounded verification to generate training data that better match the state distribution encountered during execution. We evaluate our approach on memory-dependent benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks. On RoboMME, PAL achieves a \textbf{56.05\%} success rate, outperforming the strongest baseline, FrameSamp-Modul, at 44.51\%. In real-world experiments across four manipulation tasks, \pal{} reaches \textbf{60.83\%} overall success, surpassing MemER (45.00\%) and FrameSamp-Modul (28.33\%). These results show that proactively writing future-relevant subtasks into hierarchical memory improves long-horizon visual reasoning and robot control. Code and videos can be found on our website: https://qinghangliu.github.io/pal-webpage/
authors: Qinghang Liu, Conglin Wang, Zongsheng Li, Boyong He, Han Gao, Pengcheng Wang, Tao Sun, Lige Liu, Chang Liu
bullets: Targets the heavy reasoning burden of retrieving and interpreting history during execution.
Uses hierarchical memory: a short-term visual buffer, semantic-event memory, and executable subtask list.
A high-level VLM converts streaming observations into subtasks, then selects relevant subtasks for a low-level VLA policy.
Trains memory updates with staged supervision expansion and task-grounded self-labeling.
Achieves 56.05% success on RoboMME and 60.83% overall success across four real-world manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical memory with VLM-generated subtask lists for vision-language robot manipulation fits embodied memory and VLA control.
papers.title: Plan First, Act Later: Streaming Reasoning for Executable Memory in Robot Control
papers.tldr: PAL improves long-horizon robot manipulation by planning future-relevant subtasks into executable memory before action time.

papers.abstract: Unlike question answering, where a query specifies a perceptual target, open-ended detailed captioning must determine what evidence to acquire and how to integrate it into a coherent global description. We propose Observation-Adaptive Video Captioner (OACap), a caption-centered agent that turns unsupported or missing information into targeted observation requests, uses spatiotemporal tools to acquire evidence, and iteratively verifies and revises the caption. OACap captions consistently improve performance across general video-understanding benchmarks using a fixed text-only reader. To better diagnose the information they preserve, we introduce Factual-Semantic Captioning Bench (FSCap-Bench). Its Core-Support Factuality Score (CSFS) combines claim precision with importance-aware fact coverage and responds as expected to four controlled perturbation types on 93.0-98.3% of valid caption pairs. Its Cross-Modal Semantic Round-Trip Score (CSRS) measures semantic preservation through a video-caption-video-caption round trip by matching atomic facts from source and recovered captions. Together, they connect downstream textual-memory utility with factual and semantic preservation.
authors: Hao Shi, Hong Yan, Xiaoyang Zhang, Qing Cui, Chao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of deciding what evidence to observe for open-ended, detailed video captioning.
Uses a caption-centered agent that identifies missing or unsupported information, gathers targeted spatiotemporal evidence, and revises captions iteratively.
Improves captioning performance across general video-understanding benchmarks with a fixed text-only reader.
Introduces FSCap-Bench with CSFS for importance-aware factual coverage and CSRS for cross-modal semantic preservation.
CSFS responds appropriately to four controlled perturbations in 93.0–98.3% of valid caption pairs.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces an active observation agent for detailed video captioning, relevant to video understanding and multimodal agents.
papers.title: OACap: Caption-Guided Active Observation for Detailed Video Captioning
papers.tldr: OACap actively requests and verifies visual evidence to produce more detailed, factually supported video captions, while FSCap-Bench evaluates their factual and semantic preservation.

papers.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.
authors: Kleanthis Avramidis, Ivan Tashev, Dimitra Emmanouilidou
bullets: Targets the resource and deployment limitations of increasingly large EEG foundation models.
Pretrained self-supervised on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants.
Combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder for arbitrary electrode configurations.
Encourages spatial-connectivity and narrowband-oscillation sensitivity through positional encoding and an auxiliary objective.
Matches or surpasses state of the art across sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive-load estimation, using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures.
papers.selection_reason: The paper introduces a compact EEG foundation model with 97% fewer trainable parameters, fitting the efficiency-focused topic.
papers.title: BrainCodes: A Lightweight EEG Foundation Model over Discrete Neural Codes
papers.tldr: BrainCodes is a compact EEG foundation model that learns transferable representations from discrete neural codes while supporting varied electrode layouts and efficient wearable deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are now routinely tested on theory of mind: whether they can work out what another person sees, knows, and means. A common design asks the model to report that perspective and then to act for the person, and reads a correct report beside a wrong action as a failure to use the perspective. That reading rests on a quiet assumption: that asking for the report leaves the action unchanged. We show that it does not. In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director who asks for "the largest block". Asking first which blocks the director can see raises the share of replies that choose this hidden block by 12 to 88 percentage points on six GPT models and by 17 on Qwen3.8-27B, even though the models mostly report correctly which blocks the director sees. Reasoning traces and prompt rewordings suggest why: the question shifts how the request is read, from the director's view toward the model's own. When the prompt states what the director knows and refers to, fewer than 1% of replies pair a correct report with a hidden-block choice. Any evaluation that elicits a perspective report before the action it scores needs a baseline without the question, and we deliver one: paired prompts that differ only in that question, a design any perspective-taking benchmark can adopt.
authors: Jiaxuan Guo, Xingyu Ren, Kejia Zhang, Jingxin Yang, Youran Sun, Haizhao Yang
bullets: In a rendered Director Task, a partition hides the largest block from a director requesting “the largest block.”
Asking models to report the director’s visual perspective first increased hidden-block choices by 12–88 percentage points across six GPT models and by 17 points on Qwen3.8-27B.
Models generally reported the director’s visibility correctly, suggesting the question changed how they interpreted the request rather than simply revealing a lack of perspective-taking.
Explicitly stating what the director knows and refers to reduced correct-report/hidden-choice pairings to below 1%.
The authors recommend paired prompts with and without the perspective question as a baseline for perspective-taking benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: Evaluates perspective-taking behavior in vision-language models, fitting multimodal LLM research.
papers.title: Asking What a Director Sees Can Change What Vision-Language Models Choose
papers.tldr: Asking vision-language models what a director can see can change their subsequent choice, making standard theory-of-mind evaluations confound perspective reporting with action.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires more than access to geometric tools: a reasoner must decide when direct observation is sufficient and when to reconstruct, measure, or change reference frames. We present SpatialBrain, a framework that retains experience about these decisions while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed. The key distinction is between evidence about a scene and experience about how to reason with that evidence. 3DFusionMemory fuses current-scene observations into queryable spatial relations. A Spatial Skill Library provides reusable tool procedures, and Spatial Cognition associates task conditions with experience about when and how to use memory and skills. Completed trajectories are abstracted into process records and consolidated between task blocks, allowing later decisions to draw on earlier execution without transferring scene coordinates or reference answers. Across five spatial-reasoning benchmarks, SpatialBrain improves on direct answers from the same backbone on four and ties on the fifth. Component comparisons, experience-coverage curves, and traced resource decisions characterize how the framework accumulates and uses these resources.
authors: Yifan Zhou, Ziyang Gong, Xiaojun Ye, Yifei Liu, Donggang Li, Xiaolong Zhou, Zhihang Zhong, Xue Yang
bullets: Separates scene evidence from experience about reasoning strategies.
Uses 3DFusionMemory to build queryable spatial relations from current observations.
Provides a Spatial Skill Library and Spatial Cognition for selecting reusable procedures and resources.
Abstracts completed task trajectories into process records for consolidation across task blocks.
Improves over direct answers from the same backbone on four of five benchmarks and ties on one.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial reasoning framework with a vision-language backbone, queryable 3D spatial relations, and reasoning experience growth; fits spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpatialBrain: Spatial Intelligence Growing from Experience
papers.tldr: SpatialBrain improves spatial reasoning by retaining experience about when and how to use spatial memories and tools while keeping its vision-language backbone fixed.

papers.abstract: Dynamic local community detection tracks the evolving community of designated seed nodes across graph snapshots. However, it faces two critical challenges: temporal supervision uncertainty, where sparse and outdated labels fail to provide seed-specific guidance under topology changes, and unbounded error cascades, where sequential policy transfer accumulates exploration errors over long horizons. To address these challenges, we propose DISRL, a Dual-scale Incremental Semi-supervised Reinforcement Learning framework. DISRL introduces a supervision construction module that dynamically generates seed-specific guidance from sparse known communities, and a dual-scale community exploration module that stabilizes policy evolution by decoupling short-term adaptation within temporal windows from long-term parameter consolidation across windows. Furthermore, we construct a dynamic graph benchmark with diverse community evolution scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DISRL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under various dynamic settings.
authors: Tianming Zhang, Jinxu Wang, Yixuan Zhang, Zhengyi Yang, Chenyu Hou, Bin Cao, Jing Fan
bullets: Addresses sparse, outdated labels and cascading exploration errors in dynamic community tracking.
Generates seed-specific guidance from known communities through a supervision construction module.
Separates short-term policy adaptation within temporal windows from long-term consolidation across windows.
Introduces a benchmark covering diverse community evolution scenarios.
Experiments show consistent improvement over state-of-the-art baselines across dynamic settings.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental semi-supervised policy learning over dynamic graph snapshots directly fits continual/online adaptation methods.
papers.title: DISRL: Dual-Scale Incremental Semi-Supervised Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Community Tracking
papers.tldr: DISRL tracks evolving seed-node communities by combining dynamically generated supervision with dual-scale reinforcement learning to reduce adaptation uncertainty and error accumulation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal ocean modeling remains challenging due to substantial heterogeneity in data structures, physical semantics, and spatiotemporal characteristics across satellite imagery, gridded oceanographic fields, and buoy observations. Existing approaches largely focus on task-specific ocean modeling, while learning transferable representations from heterogeneous observations remains an open problem. To address this challenge, we propose YingLan, a multimodal ocean foundation model that integrates physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding, Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC), and ocean-state evolution-aware pretraining. Specifically, the dynamic encoding mechanism generates adaptive input projections conditioned on physical semantics and observation characteristics, enabling flexible representation of heterogeneous ocean variables. STIC models multiscale spatiotemporal dependencies through cross-scale interactions of latent temporal increments. The pretraining strategy further combines masked observation reconstruction with temporal evolution objectives to facilitate the learning of coherent ocean-state representations across different prediction horizons. YingLan is implemented using MindSpore and trained on Huawei Ascend 910B NPUs, demonstrating its compatibility with domestic AI computing infrastructure. In a seven-day sea surface salinity (SSS) forecasting task conducted in the Shenzhen coastal waters, YingLan achieves an average RMSE of 0.687508 PSU, corresponding to relative error reductions of 0.58%, 5.31%, and 12.42% compared with LangYa, XiHe, and GloNet2, respectively. These results provide initial evidence of the model's effectiveness in regional ocean forecasting, while broader cross-task and cross-regional evaluations remain necessary to assess its generalization capabilities.
authors: Sen Jia, Siqi Wei, Junyu Wang, Zijun Lv, Pan Liu, Meng Xu, Xiyou Fu, Yuxi Sun, Qiang Liu, Shuyu Zhang, Lin Mu
bullets: Addresses heterogeneity across satellite imagery, gridded ocean fields, and buoy observations.
Uses physics-attribute-conditioned dynamic encoding to adapt inputs to differing physical semantics and observation characteristics.
Introduces Spatiotemporal Increment Coupling (STIC) to capture multiscale temporal and spatial dependencies.
Pretrains with masked observation reconstruction and ocean-state evolution objectives.
In Shenzhen coastal waters, it achieves 0.687508 PSU RMSE for seven-day SSS forecasting, with reported reductions versus three comparison models.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes YingLan, a multimodal foundation model for oceanography that integrates heterogeneous observations (satellite, buoy) using physics-conditioned encoding and spatiotemporal coupling.
papers.title: YingLan: A Multimodal Ocean Foundation Model for Unified Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Observations
papers.tldr: YingLan is a multimodal ocean foundation model that learns unified representations from heterogeneous observations and shows improved seven-day coastal salinity forecasting in an initial regional evaluation.

papers.abstract: Dynamic scheduling requires dispatching online arrivals while anticipating future jobs, as poor decisions can compound downstream costs under nonlinear tardiness objectives. We show that a pretrained large language model (LLM) can serve as the exogenous component of a structured world model, forecasting uncertain future job arrivals. Specifically, we exploit an afterstate decomposition, which separates known deterministic shop transitions from uncertain exogenous job arrivals, enabling the LLM to forecast only the latter through a compact belief representation. Building on this, we develop Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP), which combines an evolved, belief-conditioned dispatching strategy with short scenario-based rollouts. A surprise-triggered refresh mechanism queries the LLM only when newly observed arrivals deviate sufficiently from previous forecast, and online residual self-calibration further conditions the LLM on its recent forecast errors to handle nonstationary arrivals. Across diverse arrival distributions, AWMP reduces weighted tardiness by 6-21% on dynamic job-shop and 22-46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks, relative to the best of eight classical priority-dispatching rules.
authors: Ni Zhang, Haofeng Yuan, Jianan Zhou, Shiji Song, Zhiguang Cao
bullets: Targets dynamic job-shop scheduling, where poor dispatch decisions can compound downstream tardiness.
Uses afterstate decomposition to let the LLM model only uncertain exogenous arrivals via a compact belief representation.
Combines belief-conditioned dispatching with short scenario-based rollouts in Afterstate World-Model Planning (AWMP).
Reduces LLM queries through surprise-triggered refreshes and adapts to nonstationary arrivals using online residual self-calibration.
Across diverse arrival distributions, weighted tardiness decreases by 6–21% on dynamic job-shop and 22–46% on flexible job-shop benchmarks versus the best of eight classical rules.
papers.selection_reason: LLM-based exogenous world model for forecasting job arrivals in dynamic scheduling; fits world models broadly.
papers.title: LLM-Based Exogenous World Modeling for Dynamic Scheduling
papers.tldr: AWMP uses an LLM to forecast uncertain future job arrivals and improve online scheduling under dynamic, nonlinear tardiness costs.

papers.abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.
authors: Yongqiang Chen, Chenxi Liu, Deyu Zou, Zhenhao Chen, Tongliang Liu, Bo Han, Kun Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of low-level, surface-based program mutations without persistent units of control.
Extracts idea-level factors that explain scoring differences between programs and uses them for exploitation and exploration.
Provides theoretical conditions under which idea factors improve sample efficiency.
Improves final performance and sample efficiency by up to 5.0× across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks.
Benefits transfer across 4 other LLMs and 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench.
papers.selection_reason: Idea-level experience extraction and reuse during open-ended evolutionary search is transferable to continual/online adaptation and memory.
papers.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
papers.tldr: ExpEvolve improves evolutionary coding agents by extracting and reusing high-level ideas from program experience to guide future discovery.

papers.abstract: Language models are being explored as the interface through which space robots interpret operator commands and select among verified skills. Running them onboard calls for low-bit compression, and flight use adds requirements that generic post-training quantization leaves implicit: a fixed memory budget and storage format, a static artifact under configuration control, and behavior close to the full-precision model validated on the ground. We treat compression as a ground-segment step and study QSelect, which composes one static low-bit model from compatible AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound checkpoints by assigning each linear module to one quantizer family and scoring every substitution at the final next-token distribution. The default fidelity mode needs no labels or tuned thresholds and accepts a substitution only when the forward KL divergence from the BF16 reference decreases; an optional target-adapted mode adds answer likelihood on a small labeled set. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Llama-3.2-3B at 3 and 4 bits, composed models reach lower mean held-out perplexity than every single-family model in all six settings, and the fidelity mode lowers perplexity and KL further. In a matched scaffold, final-output scoring gives lower held-out KL than representation-similarity scoring in all 12 paired runs. With labels from training or development splits of the evaluated task families, the target-adapted mode raises 3-bit pooled accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points over the best single-family model. At 3 bits, unquantized embedding and output layers make up 43-46% of the packed artifact. All evaluations use general-domain benchmarks on a ground GPU; space-domain tasks and flight hardware are left to future work.
authors: Jia Deng, Zizhe Wang, Xin Lu, Yi Huang, Zehao Jia
bullets: Evaluates compression for space robots requiring a controlled, static artifact and behavioral fidelity to a BF16 reference.
Assigns each linear module among AWQ, GPTQ, and AutoRound variants using final next-token distribution scores.
A label-free fidelity mode accepts substitutions that reduce forward KL; an optional target-adapted mode uses labeled data.
Across three language models and 3-/4-bit settings, composed models achieve lower held-out perplexity than every single-family baseline.
Target adaptation improves pooled 3-bit accuracy on the two Llama models by 4.3 and 4.5 points; evaluations remain limited to general-domain benchmarks on ground GPUs.
papers.selection_reason: Composes low-bit quantized LLM checkpoints under a fidelity constraint for onboard deployment, directly targeting model memory efficiency.
papers.title: Compressing Onboard Language Models for Space Robots under a Behavioral-Fidelity Requirement
papers.tldr: QSelect composes compatible low-bit checkpoints into static onboard models that better preserve full-precision behavior under fixed storage constraints.

papers.abstract: Finding K most similar elements for a query in a large gallery of neural network (NN) embeddings is essential in various areas of computer science and industrial applications of artificial intelligence. This paper proposes search algorithms for structured latent spaces (LS) of NNs which allow to speed up top K item retrieval owing to O(1) complexity small candidate gallery subset search. ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models are finetuned using Latent Space Configuration (LSC) methodology to obtain new distribution of embeddings with desired geometric properties. Applying the proposed algorithms to embeddings obtained from finetuned models leads to several times speed-up over baseline exhaustive search. Specifically, we report up to 3 times speed-up on GPU and 40% speed-up on CPU compared to the baseline method GPU speed. These results are obtained for the original and reduced numbers of LS dimensions. The results show that LS dimensionality reduction allows to further accelerate the search and even improve rank-N metrics.
bullets: Targets efficient retrieval of the K most similar items from large embedding galleries.
Fine-tunes ArcFace-pretrained IResNet50 models to impose structured geometric properties on the latent space.
Uses structured latent-space search with an O(1)-complexity candidate subset instead of exhaustive comparison.
Reports up to 3× GPU speed-up and 40% CPU speed-up relative to the stated baseline.
Dimensionality reduction further accelerates retrieval and can improve rank-N metrics.
papers.selection_reason: Latent space configuration and dimensionality-reduction methods for fast top-K embedding retrieval; relevant to efficient AI serving.
papers.title: Latent space configuration for neural network finetuning, fast ranking, and embedding dimensionality reduction
papers.tldr: Latent Space Configuration reshapes neural-network embeddings to enable faster top-K similarity search, while dimensionality reduction can further improve speed and ranking quality.

papers.abstract: Managed and wild bees sustain roughly a third of the global food products, yet colonies face mounting stress from climate-change including extreme weather patterns, altered parasite and disease patterns. Timely assessment of colony condition such as understanding colony strength, brood area, honey and pollen storage, comb usage, is essential to adaptive management. However, manual hive frame inspection is slow, costly, and quality depends on scarce expertise. We present an artificial targeted intelligent system framework focusing on edge deployable pipeline that turns hive frame photographs into interpretable and action-oriented inspection report. The pipeline includes an object detector to detect biologically-meaningful comb-cell classes; detections are distilled into structured fact schema; facts are converted into constrained factual text; the text triggers a grounded knowledge-base for interpretations and recommendations. Knowledge-base entries are required to be triggerable by evidence expressed in the fact schema. We built our system based on open source FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset and favour reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general purpose frontier models. We additionally release FAIRHiveText-1K dataset that turns FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset into interchangeable facts and text interpretation of the facts, making it easy for further LLM-based research into this area. We also propose a pathway to develop the grounded knowledge-base that will be helpful in providing interpretable and actionable reports from the facts.
authors: Asaduz Zaman, Mohaimenul Azam Khan Raiaan, Malika Nisal Ratnayake
bullets: Addresses the slow, costly, and expertise-dependent nature of manual hive-frame inspection.
Detects biologically meaningful comb-cell classes and distills detections into a structured fact schema.
Generates constrained factual text that triggers interpretable recommendations from a grounded knowledge base.
Prioritizes reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general-purpose language models.
Introduces FAIRHiveText-1K and outlines a pathway for developing evidence-triggered knowledge-base entries.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a system for intelligent beekeeper assistance using computer vision and knowledge-grounded language models, fitting embodied AI and multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Computer Vision and Knowledge-Grounded Language Models for Intelligent Beekeeper Assistance
papers.tldr: An edge-deployable computer-vision and knowledge-grounded language pipeline converts hive-frame images into evidence-based, actionable beekeeper reports.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have shown strong potential for robot manipulation by jointly learning visual dynamics and executable actions. However, their video and action objectives do not explicitly constrain the 3D geometry that is crucial for precise manipulation. Recently, geometry-aware WAMs introduce depth or 4D prediction branches, whereas representation alignment methods supervise intermediate WAM features with pretrained 3D foundation models. Yet we find that such pointwise alignment benefits the video features but degrades action learning, since dense geometric feature targets overly restrict compact action features. To address this limitation, we propose Relational Geometry Forcing (RGF), which transfers geometric priors from a frozen 3D foundation model by aligning pairwise feature relations instead of pointwise features. Specifically, RGF applies three complementary relational objectives, where intra-frame and cross-view relations transfer scene geometry and multi-view correspondence to the video features, while action-temporal relations couple action dynamics to geometric scene evolution. Applied only during training, RGF requires no explicit geometry branch or extra inference module. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate the effectiveness of Relational Geometry Forcing, showing consistent gains across diverse manipulation scenarios and WAM paradigms.
authors: Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Jiabing Yang, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Jianhua Yang, Jianlou Si, Jun Huang, Jing Liu, Nianfeng Liu, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: WAMs lack explicit constraints on the 3D geometry needed for precise manipulation.
Pointwise alignment with 3D foundation-model features can help video representations but hurt compact action representations.
RGF aligns intra-frame, cross-view, and action-temporal feature relations to transfer geometry, correspondences, and scene-action dynamics.
The method is training-only and adds no explicit geometry branch or inference module.
Experiments in simulation and the real world show consistent gains across diverse manipulation settings and WAM paradigms.
papers.selection_reason: Relational geometry forcing for world action models targets manipulation, action-conditioned world dynamics, and geometry-aware multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Relational Geometry Forcing for World Action Models
papers.tldr: Relational Geometry Forcing improves world action models for precise robot manipulation by transferring 3D geometric structure through relational rather than pointwise feature alignment.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), particularly through group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), has emerged as a central paradigm for the post-training of large language models (LLMs). While RLVR is highly effective at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, it commonly induces \textit{distribution sharpening}, whereby the policy distribution becomes excessively peaked and rare-yet-correct trajectories are progressively suppressed, thus diminishing sample diversity. To this end, we promote flat-reward optima in RLVR to smooth the policy distribution. We theoretically link flat reward RLVR to reduced distribution sharpening, and empirically show improved sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy. Our method, called \texttt{Flat}-RLVR, searches for flat reward regions via sharpness-aware minimization during LLM post-training, combining this with GRPO variants to achieve better trade-offs between sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
authors: Yeonbum Kim, Hyun Kyu Lee, Sung Whan Yoon
bullets: RLVR can sharpen LLM policy distributions, suppressing rare but correct reasoning trajectories.
Flat-RLVR promotes flatter reward optima to mitigate this distribution sharpening.
The method combines sharpness-aware minimization with GRPO variants during post-training.
Theory connects flatter reward solutions with reduced distribution sharpening.
Experiments report higher sample diversity while maintaining single-attempt accuracy, balancing sampling efficiency and reasoning capacity.
papers.selection_reason: Sharpness-aware reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for LLM reasoning post-training; relevant to LLM reasoning methods.
papers.title: Flat-RLVR: Sharpness-Aware Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Reasoning Capacity in LLMs
papers.tldr: Flat-RLVR uses sharpness-aware optimization with GRPO-style RLVR to reduce policy over-concentration, improving reasoning sample diversity without sacrificing single-attempt accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large pretrained robot foundation models provide strong priors for manipulation, yet adapting them to target tasks with offline teleoperated demonstrations often fails to cover the contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical states encountered during deployment. Existing methods mitigate this issue by augmenting offline demonstrations with human-in-the-loop data or online reinforcement learning. Despite this, offline post-training adapts slowly because it cannot immediately absorb deployment experience, while online RL typically relies on value functions or auxiliary actor-critic models, increasing both training complexity and instability. We present TIDE (Training In DEployment), a human-in-the-loop online post-training system. TIDE introduces a provenance-conditioned supervised learning framework that updates the policy online from human interventions and policy-generated rollouts collected during deployment, without a learned critic, reward model, or action scorer. Across four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, TIDE improves milestone-normalized task progress and binary full-task completion over the warm-start policy and matched additional offline demonstrations, and performs comparably to the fixed-policy collection baseline while making updated checkpoints available during deployment. Each task-specific online post-training session, from the start of deployment rollouts until the final checkpoint is available, completes in less than one hour while learning and checkpoint handling run asynchronously.
authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Bozhou Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage of offline demonstrations for contact-rich, recovery, and precision-critical deployment states.
Uses provenance-conditioned supervised learning to update policies online from human- and policy-generated data.
Evaluated on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks, improving task progress and full-task completion over warm-start policies and matched offline demonstrations.
Performs comparably to a fixed-policy data-collection baseline while providing updated checkpoints during deployment.
Each task-specific post-training session completes in under one hour, with learning and checkpoint handling running asynchronously.
papers.selection_reason: Human-in-the-loop online post-training for robot manipulation directly fits embodied manipulation and deployment-time adaptation.
papers.title: Training in Deployment: Human-in-the-loop Online Post-Training for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: TIDE enables robots to improve manipulation policies during deployment by learning directly from human interventions and policy rollouts without critics, rewards, or action scorers.

papers.abstract: As-built BIM reconstruction from point clouds demands semantic, volumetric, parametric, and editable building components, beyond 2D layouts or planar abstractions. Yet existing scan-to-BIM pipelines often rely on handcrafted rules, heuristic optimization, or manual correction, while learning-based methods fall short of recovering wall thickness, opening geometry, and component-level BIM structure. We introduce CRAB, a BIM-ready cuboid reconstruction framework that encodes walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with IFC-compatible semantics and parameters. CRAB bridges point clouds and editable BIM by combining ProposalNet, which predicts coarse component cuboids, with AssemblyNet, a relation-aware Flow Matching model that refines geometry, predicts structural relationships, and enables automatic structural correction and human-guided editing. To address limited cuboid-level supervision, we extend Structured3D with component-wise cuboid annotations and construct cuboid-based procedural scenes. Experiments show CRAB surpasses floor plan and plane-based alternatives in component completeness, geometric accuracy, and generalization. For interior wall thickness estimation, CRAB achieves a mean error of 2.80 cm, with 79.50% of matched walls within 3 cm. The project page is available at https://vcc.tech/research/2026/CRAB.
authors: Haoran Xiong, Jing Wang, Shanshan Pan, Zihao Yan, Minglun Gong, Hui Huang
bullets: Targets scan-to-BIM limitations in recovering wall thickness, openings, and structured building components.
Represents walls, doors, windows, beams, and columns as compact architectural cuboids with semantic and parametric information.
Combines ProposalNet for coarse cuboid prediction with AssemblyNet for relation-aware refinement, structural correction, and human-guided editing.
Extends Structured3D with cuboid annotations and creates procedural cuboid-based scenes to support training.
Reports a 2.80 cm mean error for interior wall thickness, with 79.50% of matched walls estimated within 3 cm.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based point-cloud to BIM cuboid reconstruction with relation-aware flow matching; directly relevant to 3D scene perception.
papers.title: CRAB: Cuboid-based Representation for As-built BIM from Point Clouds
papers.tldr: CRAB reconstructs editable, IFC-compatible BIM components from point clouds using cuboid proposals and relation-aware geometric refinement.

papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) understand music, yet struggle to locate a described moment in time. We ask whether this reflects missing temporal information or a bottleneck in how the time span is extracted. Using a paired-query probe built from Slakh2100 stem activations, we attach a state query (e.g., ``only piano and bass are playing'') and a change query (e.g., ``the guitar drops out, leaving piano and bass'') to the same span and vary how much preceding audio the model is shown. Across frozen LALMs, three ways of extracting the span ask different questions: full-track prompting asking whether the model can say when; windowed yes/no scoring asking whether it verifies the moment when handed the segment, and whether it needs what came before; attention asking whether it can find the moment on its own. State queries score above baseline without context, while change queries improve with preceding context in most short-segment models; 30s padded encoders show no comparable recovery. Prompting and attention expose almost none of this. Prompting failures thus understate what LALMs can verify, though not what they can locate, by an amount set by query type and encoder.
bullets: LALMs struggle to identify when a described musical moment occurs, raising questions about missing temporal information versus extraction bottlenecks.
A paired-query probe compares state descriptions (what is playing) with change descriptions (what just stopped) over the same audio span and varying preceding context.
State queries perform above baseline without context, while change queries usually benefit from preceding audio in short-segment models.
Full-track prompting and attention reveal little of this contextual ability; windowed yes/no scoring exposes more verification capacity.
Thirty-second padded encoders do not show comparable recovery, indicating that effects depend on query type and encoder design.
papers.selection_reason: Analysis of temporal information extraction in frozen audio-language models; meaningful for multimodal model understanding.
papers.title: Heard But Not Said: Prompting Understates Temporal Information of Musical Moments in Frozen Large Audio-Language Models
papers.tldr: Frozen large audio-language models can often verify musical states, but prompting and attention substantially understate their ability to use temporal context and locate musical changes.

papers.abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization.
